ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
As shown in the figure, the two series resistors $R_{1}=12k\Omega$, $R_{2}{=}36k\Omega$, and the voltage across terminals $A$ and $B$ remains constant at 15V.

1. What are the voltages across $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$?
2. If the internal resistance of the voltmeter $V$ is $12k\Omega$, what are the readings of the voltmeter when S is in contact with $C$ and $D$, respectively?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The left side of the figure is labeled with upper terminal A and lower terminal B, and a voltage U is applied between A and B. In the middle is a vertical branch; the upper part is resistor R1 and the lower part is resistor R2, the two are connected in series, and connected between the two terminals A and B. The midpoint of R1 and R2 is connected to the right to voltmeter V, and then connected to switch S. The upper contact C on the right side is connected to the upper wire, that is, node A; the lower contact D on the right side is connected to the lower wire, that is, node B. Reasoning calculation: It is known that R1=12 kΩ, R2=36 kΩ, U_AB=15 V. 1. When not considering the voltmeter load, R1 and R2 are in series, and the voltage is distributed according to resistance. The total resistance is 12 kΩ+36 kΩ=48 kΩ. Therefore the voltage across R1 is 15×12/48=3.75 V; the voltage across R2 is 15×36/48=11.25 V. 2. The internal resistance of the voltmeter Rv=12 kΩ. When S is connected to C, the voltmeter in the figure is connected across the two ends of R1, therefore R1 and the voltmeter are in parallel: R1||Rv=12 kΩ||12 kΩ=6 kΩ. This 6 kΩ is then in series with R2=36 kΩ, and the voltmeter reading is the voltage of the upper parallel branch: 15×6/(6+36)=15/7 V. When S is connected to D, the voltmeter is connected across the two ends of R2, therefore R2 and the voltmeter are in parallel: R2||Rv=36 kΩ||12 kΩ=9 kΩ. This 9 kΩ is in series with R1=12 kΩ, and the voltmeter reading is the voltage of the lower parallel branch: 15×9/(12+9)=45/7 V.
